uncertainty_flags: Per-token probability shifts may conflate immediate-token effects with preceding context/state (A1).
Moderate correlations (.32–.43) with SVM coefficients are supportive but far from conclusive validation (A3).
Bayesian 95% HDIs overlap zero for key contrasts; directional posterior mass measures require cautious interpretation (A6).
Synthetic probes may be out-of-distribution; no explicit OOD checks reported (A4).
Classification performance reported on a single split without variance estimation limits confidence in LSTM > SVM claim (A7).
Pretrained embeddings and manual cleaning could introduce systematic biases that affect probes (A8, A9).
alternative_interpretations: Moderate correlations between LSTM token shifts and SVM coefficients could reflect both models picking up on high-frequency topical tokens or dataset artifacts (e.g., value words) rather than semantic justification structures.
Directional posterior mass (e.g., 99.8%) with HDI overlapping zero might arise from a narrow but asymmetric posterior tail; practical effect size could be negligible even if direction is probable.

Model increases in male-treatment probability for self-focused probes could stem from co-occurring lexical patterns in training data (e.g., certain verbs or pronouns) rather than a coherent self-focus semantic dimension.

Synthetic probes might inadvertently trigger model heuristics (e.g., phrase templates strongly associated with treatment prompt) that amplify small lexical cues and produce apparent gender differences.
transparency_notes: Training/test split is reported (85/15) but no seeds, number of epochs, early-stopping criteria, or variance across runs are provided.
Details on manual text cleaning procedures are sparse—documenting who performed edits and what operations were applied would aid reproducibility.
Priors in Bayesian models are stated as 'standard normal' but exact parameterization, sampling diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample size), and posterior predictive checks are not reported.
Embedding treatment for OOV tokens is described (initialized to 0 and trainable) but counts of OOV probe tokens and their influence on results are not given.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The output-level sequential-probing approach is relatively uncommon compared to hidden-state analyses; lack of direct analogs in retrieved literature signals methodological innovation but does not, by itself, establish validity—empirical robustness checks are required.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If per-token softmax outputs are verified to reflect token-local contributions via controlled ablations and context-conditional tests, then sequential-probing can validly map learned dimensions.

If synthetic probes are shown to fall within the model's training distribution (via embedding distance and performance similarity to real sentences), probe-based inferences are more likely to generalize to natural essays.
If Bayesian model diagnostics (posterior predictive checks, prior sensitivity) show stable effect direction and practical effect sizes, the psychological inferences gain credibility.
If classification superiority of LSTM over SVM is robust across multiple splits and hyperparameter settings, downstream probe inferences rest on a stronger foundation.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Moderately novel but related to existing interpretability work
novelty_lenses.rationale: The idea of probing models with inputs echoes psycholinguistic stimulus methods and prior activation-inspection techniques; using output softmax per timestep and CLR+Bayesian inference is a novel combination applied to a psycholinguistic hypothesis.
evidence: Related work (Karpathy et al., Hermans & Schrauwen) inspects internal states; this paper focuses on output-level probing.
CLR transform and Bayesian crossed-effects model borrow established statistical practice but applied to model outputs.
uncertainty_flags: Extent to which this pipeline generalizes beyond this dataset and architecture remains untested.

novelty_lenses.rationale: If sequential output probing is shown to reliably reflect learned semantic dimensions across architectures and datasets, it offers a practical interpretability route that avoids inspecting complex internal state dynamics and could be widely adopted.
evidence: Paper demonstrates an applied pipeline and validation step correlating with SVM, plus use in an applied psychological question.
Output-level probing requires fewer model-internal access mechanisms and could be applied to black-box models if they expose per-token outputs.
uncertainty_flags: Current evidence is limited to a single dataset, architecture, and probe design; major validation gaps exist (A1, A4, A7).

confidence_interval.rationale: I report high confidence in observations about what the paper actually did and the weaknesses that follow directly from reported methods and results (hence many flagged issues are high-confidence). However, quantifying the ultimate validity of the interpretability claims requires experiments not present in the manuscript, so a precise numerical confidence about final claims' correctness cannot be narrowly bounded; hence a full 0–1 interval with rationale is provided.

consensus_findings: The paper presents a coherent, hypothesis-driven pipeline: train an LSTM classifier on essays, record per-timestep softmax outputs at test time (sequential-probing), validate token-level signals against a linear SVM baseline, construct synthetic sentence probes that vary justification type, transform compositional outputs with a centered log-ratio (CLR), and fit Bayesian multilevel models to estimate directional contrasts (Fpref).
CLR transformation and multilevel Bayesian modeling with crossed random effects are appropriate, principled choices for handling compositional softmax outputs and stimulus sampling variability.

Reported empirical facts are sufficiently documented in the manuscript: a single-split LSTM macro-F1 = 0.60 vs SVM macro-F1 = 0.53 (85/15 split), moderate Pearson correlations (r ≈ 0.32–0.43) between averaged LSTM token probability shifts and SVM token coefficients, and probe-derived posterior summaries indicating directional support (male self-focused: Fpref mean ≈ -0.23 with 99.8% posterior mass in the hypothesized direction but 95% HDI overlapping zero; female other-focused: Fpref mean ≈ 0.06 with 74% posterior mass and HDI overlapping zero).

All reviewers agree that the method is conceptually novel/interesting (output-level sequential probing as a behavioral/experimental-style interpretability tool) and that it could be useful if validated with additional robustness checks.
disagreements: Interpretive strength: Reviewers disagree on how strongly to treat the probe-based psychological claims. Some view the directional posterior mass (e.g., 99.8%) as noteworthy evidence of a learned signal; others consider the same result weak because the 95% HDI includes zero and because probe/OOD and modeling sensitivities are unresolved.

Novelty framing: Some reviewers treat the approach as a practically useful, incremental advancement relative to hidden-state inspection, while others characterize it as a potentially disruptive reframing that needs more validation before being treated as an established interpretability method.

Sufficiency of correlation validation: Some reviewers accept the moderate SVM–LSTM token correlations as a meaningful validation step; others see them as necessary but insufficient and insist on causal/ablation tests before treating sequential-probing as validated.
uncertainty_hotspots: Per-token attribution: Whether softmax changes at timestep t can be causally attributed to the immediately preceding token (assumption A1). Lack of ablation or controlled-context diagnostics leaves open the possibility that observed shifts reflect longer-range context or gating dynamics rather than token-local information.

Probe distributional validity (OOD risk): Whether the synthetic sentence fragments ('V is important to me because J') lie sufficiently within the model's training distribution so that probe responses reflect learned corpus signals rather than out-of-distribution artifacts or embedding priors (assumption A4).

Averaging across contexts: Aggregating per-token probability shifts into single token-level averages may obscure heterogeneous/context-dependent effects (assumption A2) and drive spurious correlations with SVM coefficients.

Robustness to modeling choices and randomness: Classification performance, token-shift patterns, and probe inferences are reported for single splits and a single model instantiation; sensitivity to random seeds, train/test splits, embedding initialization (GloVe vs random), architecture variants, and hyperparameter tuning is not reported (assumption A7, A9).

Bayesian model specification and interpretation: The use of directional posterior mass alongside 95% HDIs that include zero raises interpretive ambiguity (assumption A6). Sensitivity to priors, random-effects structure, and sampling diagnostics (R-hat, ESS, posterior predictive checks) is not provided.

Preprocessing confounds: Manual text cleaning and embedding treatment (zero init for OOV) are underspecified and may introduce dataset artifacts correlated with gender or condition (assumption A8, A9).
model_diversity_effects: Structure-analyst perspective emphasized the logical coherence of the pipeline and valued the validation step correlating LSTM outputs with SVM coefficients; it flagged chain vulnerabilities (token attribution, probe OOD) but treated the pipeline as conceptually consistent.

Methodology-auditor perspective prioritized reproducibility and causal validation: requested ablations, multiple-split performance estimates, explicit Stan diagnostics, and code/data release; saw the SVM correlation as necessary but insufficient.

Novelty-assessor (incremental) perspective viewed the method as a meaningful incremental contribution that adapts psycholinguistic experimental logic to model probing; tempered enthusiasm with demands for robustness.

Novelty-assessor (disruptive) perspective highlighted conceptual novelty (treating model as experimental subject) and potential practical utility, while stressing that novelty increases need for explicit limitations and validation.

Claim-verifier perspective focused on evidence and uncertainty, synthesizing the empirical numbers and pointing out that many inferential steps depend on untested assumptions. Across roles, differences center on emphasis: logical coherence vs reproducibility vs novelty potential vs strict evidential thresholds.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Center decisions on whether the work provides a useful, reproducible methodological contribution and whether the empirical claims are presented with appropriate caveats. Prioritize requesting a focused set of robustness and validation experiments before further external dissemination: (1) token-locality diagnostics (controlled-context ablations and leave-one-out/occlusion tests) to test whether per-timestep softmax shifts meaningfully reflect the target token's contribution; (2) probe-sensitivity and distributional checks (compare synthetic probes to matched real-sentence fragments, compute embedding/perplexity distances, include control/negative probes); (3) robustness for classification performance (k-fold or repeated-split evaluations with reported variance and multiple random seeds) and repeated LSTM trainings to show stability of token-shift patterns; (4) Bayesian model transparency (report priors, Stan diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, and prior sensitivity analyses; consider ROPE or Bayes factor reporting to contextualize directional mass when HDIs overlap zero); (5) preprocessing/embedding sensitivity (re-run critical analyses with alternative embedding initialization and without manual cleaning or document cleaning procedures and verify probe tokens are not zero-initialized). Ask authors to share code, processed probe lists, model checkpoints or seeds, data splits (or scripts to reconstruct them), and Stan model code to enable reproduction and independent validation. Keep editor as the arbiter to weigh whether the requested additional analyses suffice for claims to be presented with appropriate qualification; do not conflate methodological novelty with final empirical validation in place of these checks.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidential support and interpretability claims, perform and report the following targeted analyses and documentation: (1) Token-locality experiments: present controlled-context tests where the same target justification token/bigram appears in multiple identical preceding contexts (and in empty/neutral contexts) to quantify variance of per-token shifts; run occlusion/leave-one-out and gradient-based attributions (integrated gradients or influence functions) as cross-checks. (2) Probe realism and OOD checks: extract matching clauses from held-out real essays and compare responses to synthetic probes; compute embedding- or perplexity-based distances between probes and natural sentences; include control probes (nonsense or implausible justifications) to show baseline sensitivity. (3) Robustness of classification and probing: report macro-F1 means and SDs across multiple random train/test splits and multiple model initializations; repeat key probe analyses across several seeds and at least one alternative architecture or embedding initialization to show stability. (4) Bayesian sensitivity and diagnostics: provide full Stan diagnostics (R-hat, ESS), posterior plots, posterior predictive checks, and prior-sensitivity analyses; consider reporting ROPE analyses or Bayes factors and translate CLR-contrast effect sizes back into probability-space magnitudes for practical interpretation. (5) Preprocessing transparency: document manual cleaning rules and show checks for systematic differences by gender/condition; report counts of OOV probe tokens and whether any probes used zero-initialized embeddings. (6) Release artifacts: publish code, probe item lists, model seeds/checkpoints, Stan code, and (where permissible) processed data splits or scripts to recreate them. In reporting, contextualize empirical claims conservatively: present probe-derived psychological inferences as model-detected signals that require triangulation rather than direct claims about human cognition, and explicitly state limitations around probe OOD, averaging context effects, and embedding biases.
transparency_report: Missing/insufficiently reported items identified by reviewers: random seeds and number of training restarts; variance of classification metrics across splits; full hyperparameter grids and chosen hyperparameters for both LSTM and SVM; exact train/validation/test split indices or reproducible split scripts.

Bayesian-model-related omissions: exact prior parameterizations (beyond 'standard normal'), Stan sampling diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample sizes), posterior predictive checks, and prior-sensitivity analyses were not included.

Data preprocessing lacks detail: the manual text-cleaning protocol (who performed edits, what counted as 'gross' errors, whether editors were blind to labels) is not documented, and counts of OOV tokens/zero-initialized embeddings for probe tokens are not reported.

Probe artifact disclosure: full lists of the 195 self-focused and 195 other-focused sentence fragments, their token frequencies in training data, and any filtering criteria are not provided in the manuscript.
No public code repository, model checkpoints, or Stan model code are referenced; reviewers flagged this as an obstacle to reproducibility.
epistemic_limits: The method infers dataset-level signals via model behavior, not direct properties of human authors: model outputs reflect a combination of training-corpus patterns, learned parameters influenced by embedding priors, preprocessing artifacts, and architectural inductive biases. Correlation between LSTM token-shift averages and SVM coefficients indicates shared signal but does not establish causality or semantic equivalence. Synthetic-probe responses can only be interpreted as evidence that the trained model responds systematically to crafted inputs; extrapolation from model responses to claims about human psychological tendencies requires triangulation with in-distribution evidence (natural essay clauses, human annotations) and robustness checks. Posterior-directional probability (proportion of posterior mass with a given sign) can provide one perspective on directionality, but when the 95% HDI overlaps zero it indicates substantial uncertainty about effect magnitude; interpreting such posterior asymmetries as strong empirical support without sensitivity analyses risks overstatement. Finally, absence of multiple seeds, splits, and diagnostic reporting limits confidence in the stability and generalizability of the reported findings; until ablation and robustness checks are conducted, claims about the interpretability method's general validity and about psychological conclusions should be treated as provisional and contingent on further validation.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes and applies an output-level interpretability pipeline: train an LSTM to classify values-affirmation essays (gender × condition), record the model's softmax outputs at each token (sequential-probing), validate averaged token-level probability shifts by correlating them with linear SVM token coefficients, probe the trained model with synthetic sentence fragments that vary justification type (self-focused vs other-focused), apply a centered log-ratio (CLR) transform to class-probability vectors, and fit Bayesian multilevel models (crossed random effects) to estimate directional contrasts (Fpref) testing psychological hypotheses. Empirically, the paper reports a single-split LSTM macro-F1 = 0.60 vs SVM .53, moderate token-level correlations (r ≈ 0.32–0.43) with SVM coefficients, and probe-derived posterior summaries that are directionally consistent with a stronger male self-focused signal (Fpref mean ≈ -0.23; 95% HDI overlaps zero but ~99.8% posterior mass in the direction) and a weak female other-focused tendency (Fpref mean ≈ 0.06; 74% posterior mass).
strengths: Coherent, hypothesis-driven pipeline that links classifier training, behavioral-style probing, compositional transformation (CLR), and Bayesian multilevel inference tailored to stimulus sampling.
Appropriate recognition of compositionality: CLR transform applied to softmax outputs before statistical modeling and use of crossed random effects to model stimulus-level variability.
Practical validation step: correlating averaged LSTM token probability shifts with SVM token coefficients provides an external baseline check rather than relying only on qualitative examples.

Novel, portable conceptual framing: treating a trained model as an experimental subject and probing it with designed linguistic stimuli is a clear, low-intrusion interpretability strategy that may be useful to applied researchers.
limitations: Per-token attribution not demonstrated: the central interpretability assumption that per-timestep softmax changes can be causally attributed to the immediately preceding token (assumption A1) is untested. No controlled-context ablations, leave-one-out token perturbations, or other causal-locality diagnostics are reported, so token-level interpretations may conflate immediate-token content with longer-range context or state dynamics.

Probe distributional validity (OOD risk) unassessed: synthetic probes ('V is important to me because J') are assumed to approximate treatment-essay contexts (assumption A4) but no quantitative or qualitative checks (e.g., embedding/perplexity distances, matched real-sentence comparisons, or control probes) are provided, leaving open that probe responses may reflect out-of-distribution behavior or embedding priors rather than learned essay signals.

Single-split performance and limited robustness reporting: classification comparisons (LSTM vs SVM) are point estimates on one 85/15 split with no variance across random seeds or splits; similarly, probe-derived contrasts are shown for a single model instance without replication across initializations, architectures, or embedding treatments (assumptions A7, A9).

Bayesian interpretive ambiguity: several key contrasts have 95% HDIs overlapping zero while authors emphasize directional posterior mass (e.g., 99.8%). Sensitivity to priors, model diagnostics (R-hat, ESS), posterior predictive checks, ROPE/Bayes-factor analyses and effect-size translation to probability-space are not reported, complicating judgment about practical significance (assumption A6).
open_questions: Can the authors present token-locality diagnostics (concrete experiments): e.g., feed the same target justification token/bigram in identical neutral preceding contexts vs varied preceding contexts, perform token-occlusion/leave-one-out perturbations, or compute integrated gradients/local influence metrics to triangulate whether per-timestep output shifts reflect the current token's contribution?

How do synthetic probes compare to in-distribution examples? Please report embedding-distance or language-model perplexity comparisons between probes and held-out treatment sentences, and show model outputs for matched natural clauses (or real essay excerpts) containing the same justification bigrams to verify probe realism.

Please provide robustness checks for the reported classifier advantage and probe effects: macro-F1 means ± SD across multiple random train/test splits and LSTM initializations; repeat key probe analyses across at least several seeds and (optionally) one alternate architecture or embedding initialization (random vs GloVe).

What are the Bayesian model diagnostics and sensitivity results? Please report exact priors used, R-hat and effective sample sizes, posterior predictive checks, and prior-sensitivity or ROPE analyses so that readers can assess whether directional posterior mass is robust to modeling choices.
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers agree the pipeline is logically coherent and conceptually interesting: sequential softmax probing plus CLR and multilevel Bayesian modeling is a plausible, novel combination for hypothesis-driven interpretability.
CLR transform and the use of crossed random effects are appropriate statistical choices for compositional outputs and stimulus sampling variability.

Empirical facts reported in the manuscript are consistent across reviewers: single-split macro-F1 values, moderate SVM–LSTM token correlations, and probe-derived posterior summaries with directional asymmetry but HDIs that overlap zero.
disagreement_snapshot: Strength of interpretive evidence: some reviewers view high directional posterior mass (e.g., 99.8%) as noteworthy evidence of a learned signal, while others regard the same result as weak because the 95% HDI includes zero and because probe OOD and token-locality concerns are unresolved.

Novelty characterization: reviewers differ on whether this is a practically incremental methodological contribution (low-risk innovation) or a potentially disruptive reframing that requires substantial validation before adoption.

Sufficiency of current validation: disagreement exists about whether moderate correlations with an SVM baseline suffice as validation for sequential-probing; some call for additional causal/ablation tests while others find the correlation a reasonable first check.
uncertainty_snapshot: High uncertainty that per-token softmax shifts reflect token-local causal contributions (token vs context confound).
Moderate uncertainty that synthetic probes lie sufficiently in-distribution such that model responses generalize to natural essays (probe OOD risk).
Uncertainty about stability of classification and probe findings across seeds/splits/architectures and sensitivity to embedding/preprocessing choices (manual cleaning, GloVe OOV handling).
Ambiguity in interpreting Bayesian directional mass when credible intervals overlap zero without sensitivity analyses or model diagnostics.
source_trace: Karpathy et al. (2015) 'Visualizing and Understanding RNNs' — precedent for probing recurrent nets via internal-state inspection; cited in manuscript related work and reviewers' comparative analysis.
Linzen et al. (2016) 'Assessing LSTMs on syntactic dependencies' — conceptual analogy: targeted synthetic stimuli used to probe model knowledge (syntax-focused probes).
Aitchison (1986) — foundational reference for centered log-ratio transform applied to compositional data (manuscript cites CLR usage in Methods Section 3.3).

Baayen et al. (2008) and Westfall et al. (2016) — methodological standards motivating use of crossed random effects for stimulus sampling in psycholinguistic mixed-effects models (manuscript follows these practices per Section 3.3).

Manuscript Results (Section 3.1–3.3) — reported empirical numbers used throughout: LSTM macro-F1 = .60; SVM macro-F1 = .53; Pearson r ≈ .32–.43 for token correlations; Fpref posterior summaries (means, HDIs, posterior mass percentages) for self- and other-focused probes.
transparency_notes: Missing or incomplete reporting that hinders reproducibility and assessment: random seeds and number of training restarts; variability of classification metrics across splits; exact hyperparameter settings and tuning procedures for both LSTM and SVM; full probe item lists and token frequency counts; documentation of manual text-cleaning procedures and whether cleaning was blind to gender/condition; counts of OOV/zero-initialized embeddings and whether any probe tokens were OOV; explicit Stan model code, priors, and sampling diagnostics (R-hat, ESS); and availability of code/data splits or scripts to reproduce analyses. Reviewers request these materials to validate robustness and to run the targeted ablations and sensitivity checks described above.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request a focused set of reproducibility and validation experiments before further external dissemination of interpretability and substantive psychological claims. Required analyses should include: (1) token-locality diagnostics (controlled-context ablations, occlusion/leave-one-out tests, gradient-based attributions); (2) probe realism and OOD checks (embedding/perplexity distances, matched real-sentence comparisons, negative-control probes); (3) robustness of classification and probe results across multiple random splits and model initializations (report means and variability); (4) Bayesian-model transparency (exact priors, Stan diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, prior sensitivity, ROPE or Bayes factors); and (5) documentation and sensitivity analyses for preprocessing and embedding choices (manual cleaning protocol, alternative embedding initializations). Require release of code, probe lists, Stan code, and split scripts or seeds to enable replication. Use these deliverables to judge whether interpretability claims are adequately validated and whether empirical inferences are appropriately qualified.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript, perform and report the following targeted steps: (1) Token-locality validation: run controlled-context experiments where the same target justification token/bigram is placed into identical neutral preceding contexts and into varied contexts; run occlusion/leave-one-out perturbations and at least one gradient-based attribution (e.g., integrated gradients) to triangulate token contribution. (2) Probe validity checks: extract matched clauses from held-out essays containing the same justification bigrams and compare model outputs to synthetic probes; compute embedding-space and language-model perplexity distances between probes and real sentences; include negative-control probes (implausible or shuffled justifications). (3) Robustness and replication: report macro-F1 averages ± SD over repeated random train/test splits (or k-fold CV) and repeat probe experiments across multiple LSTM random seeds; test sensitivity to embedding initialization (random vs GloVe) and, if feasible, one alternate architecture. (4) Bayesian transparency: publish exact priors, Stan model code, R-hat/ESS diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, and prior-sensitivity/ROPE analyses; provide effect-size translations back into raw probability units for practical interpretation. (5) Preprocessing documentation: describe manual-cleaning procedures, provide counts of OOV tokens and whether probe tokens were zero-initialized, and (if significant) re-run analyses without manual cleaning or with documented automated cleaning to test sensitivity. (6) Artifact release: share code, probe lists, model seeds/checkpoints (subject to data-sharing permissions), and scripts to reproduce splits and figures. In the manuscript text, explicitly frame psychological conclusions as model-detected signals requiring triangulation with in-distribution evidence and emphasize limitations introduced by potential OOD probe responses and averaging across contexts.
human_facing_meta_review.comments: Summary: The paper presents a clear, hypothesis-driven pipeline that treats a trained LSTM as an experimental subject by recording per-timestep softmax outputs, validating token-level signals against an SVM baseline, probing with synthetic sentence fragments (self- vs other-focused justifications), applying a CLR transform to compositional probabilities, and fitting Bayesian multilevel models with crossed random effects to estimate directional contrasts (Fpref). Reported empirical results are: single-split LSTM macro-F1 = 0.60 vs SVM = 0.53; moderate token-level correlations (r ≈ 0.32–0.43) between averaged LSTM shifts and SVM coefficients; and probe-derived posterior summaries consistent with stronger male self-focused signal and a weak female other-focused tendency, though credible intervals overlap zero for key contrasts. Strengths: The pipeline is logically coherent and novel in combining output-level sequential probing with psycholinguistic-style stimulus design and compositional Bayesian modeling; CLR and crossed random effects are principled choices; the SVM correlation is a useful external validation step; and framing the model as an experimental subject is a practical, accessible interpretability strategy. Limitations: (1) Per-token attribution is not causally established—no ablation or controlled-context diagnostics are reported, so per-timestep attributions may conflate token content with preceding context. (2) Synthetic-probe distributional validity is unassessed—no embedding/perplexity or matched natural-sentence comparisons are shown, raising OOD risk. (3) Classification and probe results are shown for a single split/model instance with no reported variability across seeds or splits; robustness across initializations, architectures, or embedding treatments is unknown. (4) Bayesian interpretation relies on directional posterior mass despite HDIs overlapping zero and lacks diagnostic/sensitivity reporting (priors, R-hat, ESS, posterior predictive checks). Open Questions: (1) Can you provide token-locality experiments (controlled preceding context, occlusion/leave-one-out, integrated gradients) to test whether per-timestep softmax shifts reflect the current token? (2) Do synthetic probes match in-distribution sentences? Please provide embedding/perplexity distances and model outputs for matched natural clauses from held-out essays. (3) What is the variance of macro-F1 and probe contrasts across multiple random splits and model seeds? (4) Provide full Bayesian diagnostics (exact priors, R-hat, ESS, posterior predictive checks) and prior-sensitivity/ROPE analyses to justify directional interpretations when HDIs span zero. Transparency: The manuscript omits key reproducibility artifacts: training seeds and restart counts, variability across splits, full hyperparameter grids and chosen settings, probe item lists and frequencies, manual-cleaning protocol, counts of OOV/zero-initialized embeddings for probe tokens, and Stan model code plus sampling diagnostics. Reviewers request these materials and urge release of code and processed splits where permissible. Overall, the approach is conceptually promising and could be practically useful if the core validation gaps (token-locality, probe OOD, robustness to randomness and preprocessing, and Bayesian diagnostics) are addressed; until then, substantive psychological inferences should be presented as model-detected signals that require triangulation rather than as direct evidence about human authors.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence bounds reflect moderate certainty that the pipeline is conceptually coherent and the reported empirical numbers are correctly extracted from the manuscript, but substantial uncertainty remains about the validity and generalizability of the interpretability claims due to untested assumptions (token-locality, probe OOD, single-split reporting, and Bayesian sensitivity). The lower bound captures the possibility that unresolved methodological gaps materially weaken interpretive claims; the upper bound reflects reasonable confidence that, with the requested robustness checks and transparency, the approach could be validated as a useful, novel interpretability method.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
